blocks.text: HTTP methods form a semantic contract about what kind of operation a request actually performs, this topic goes deeper into GET, POST, PUT, PATCH, and DELETE specifically, and why LLM completion APIs overwhelmingly rely on just one of them.

This topic covers what each HTTP method semantically signals, which specific methods LLM APIs actually use and why, and how to choose the right method correctly when building your own API that wraps or extends a provider LLM API.
1. HTTP Methods as a Semantic Contract

blocks.alt: HTTP Methods as a Semantic Contract
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785473974145-393907762.png

Each HTTP method carries an implicit meaning beyond just being a technical detail, using the right method for a given operation makes an API predictable and easier to reason about, both for the people building against it and for tooling that relies on these conventions.
2. The Five Common Methods and What They Signal

blocks.alt: The Five Common Methods and What They Signal
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785473974145-679452407.png

GET retrieves data and should never cause a side effect, POST creates something new or triggers an action, PUT replaces an entire resource, PATCH updates only part of one, and DELETE removes a resource entirely, this is standard REST convention, not something specific to LLM APIs, but it matters for understanding why LLM APIs are built the way they are.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Method","Semantic Meaning"],"rows":[["GET","Retrieve data, no side effects"],["POST","Create something new or trigger an action"],["PUT / PATCH","Replace or partially update an existing resource"],["DELETE","Remove a resource"]]}

blocks.text: 3. GET for Listing Available Models
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785473974145-685376573.png

This connects directly to the earlier REST APIs topic, listing which models a provider currently makes available is a pure data retrieval with no side effects, exactly matching GET semantics, this is one of the few genuinely GET-based operations in a typical LLM API.
4. POST for Generating a Completion
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785473974145-513102711.png

Generating a response triggers real computation and consumes real resources, this is not a pure retrieval, it genuinely matches POST semantics, triggering an action, which is exactly why nearly every LLM completion call across every major provider uses POST.
5. PUT or PATCH for Updating a Stored Configuration

blocks.alt: PUT or PATCH for Updating a Stored Configuration
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785473974145-350779469.png

Some providers let you create and store a reusable assistant configuration, a specific system prompt and settings saved under an identifier, updating that stored configuration matches PUT, replacing it entirely, or PATCH, updating only specific fields, semantics rather than the POST semantics used for generation itself.
6. DELETE for Removing a Stored Resource

blocks.alt: DELETE for Removing a Stored Resource
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785473974302-954531095.png

Providers offering file upload or persistent resource storage, for use with retrieval features covered in the earlier RAG Prompting module, typically expose a DELETE endpoint for removing that stored resource, matching standard DELETE semantics exactly.
7. Why LLM Completion APIs Are Overwhelmingly POST-Based

The core act of generating a response is fundamentally an action with real computational cost and a result to return, not a pure data retrieval, this is precisely why POST dominates LLM API usage even though GET, PUT, PATCH, and DELETE all have their place for the more peripheral, resource management parts of a provider API.

blocks.title: This mirrors general REST API design outside AI entirely
blocks.content: The same reasoning that makes POST the right choice for triggering an expensive computation applies identically in any REST API, not something unique to language models specifically.

blocks.text: 8. Choosing the Right Method for Your Own Wrapper API

blocks.alt: Choosing the Right Method for Your Own Wrapper API
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785473974303-442161663.png

This connects directly to the API architecture topic covered in an earlier module, if you build your own backend API that wraps a provider LLM API, applying the same correct method semantics, POST for triggering generation, GET for retrieving stored results, keeps your own API just as predictable and easy to reason about as the provider API it wraps.
9. A Worked Example Across Several Endpoints

A complete application might use GET to list available models, POST to generate a chat completion, PUT to update a saved assistant configuration, and DELETE to remove an uploaded reference file, each operation genuinely matches the semantic meaning of its chosen method.
Worked Example

A developer building their own internal API wrapper around a provider LLM API initially uses POST for every single operation, including retrieving a list of previously generated responses, this works but confuses other engineers on the team who expect a pure retrieval to use GET.

Restructuring the wrapper API to use GET specifically for retrieval operations and reserving POST for operations that actually trigger generation or create something new brings the API in line with standard expectations, making it immediately more intuitive for the rest of the team to use correctly.
Common Mistakes

items: Using POST for a pure data retrieval operation that has no side effects and should be a GET
Assuming every LLM API operation is POST-based without checking the specific endpoint you are actually calling
Not applying consistent method semantics when building your own wrapper API around a provider API
Confusing PUT, which replaces an entire resource, with PATCH, which updates only part of one

blocks.text: Practice

Take a hypothetical API you might build for managing saved AI assistant configurations, list operations, create a new one, update one, delete one, and assign the semantically correct HTTP method to each operation.
Key Takeaway

HTTP methods carry a semantic meaning beyond technical detail, GET for pure retrieval, POST for creating or triggering an action, PUT and PATCH for updates, and DELETE for removal, LLM completion calls are overwhelmingly POST-based since generation is a genuine action with real cost, and applying this same correct semantics matters just as much when building your own wrapper API around a provider one.
